questions.stem: A node of a singly linked list holds:
options: a value and a reference to the next node
a value and its index in the list
a value and references to every later node
only a value; the list stores the order separately
questions.explanation: The order is in the links themselves; there are no indices (b) and no separate order (d).

questions.stem: Reading ll[i] on a linked list of n nodes costs:
questions.explanation: Follow next i times from head: O(i), O(n) in the worst case.

questions.stem: push_front costs:
questions.explanation: Two reference assignments, independent of n. "Amortised" (c) describes the dynamic array's append, not this.

questions.stem: append on a singly linked list without a tail reference costs:
questions.explanation: It must walk to the last node first. A tail reference makes it O(1).

questions.stem: Which operation is O(1) on a linked list but O(n) on a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: Front insertion: two references here; every element shifts in an array.

questions.stem: Which operation is O(1) on a dynamic array but O(n) on a linked list?
questions.explanation: Indexing: address arithmetic in an array, a walk in a list. len (d) is O(1) in both — because the list keeps _size.

questions.stem: In push_front, why must new.next = self.head come before self.head = new?
options: Python evaluates assignments right to left
Done the other way round, new.next would point to new itself and the rest of the list would be lost
It is only a style convention
questions.explanation: After self.head = new, new.next = self.head makes the node point at itself, and the old first node is no longer referenced by anything. Python evaluates each assignment's right-hand side first (a), but that is not the reason for the order of two separate statements.

questions.stem: To remove a node from a singly linked list, you need a reference to:
questions.explanation: Only the predecessor holds the reference that must be redirected around the removed node.

questions.stem: Which node is the special case in remove(value) without a sentinel?
options: none — there is no special case
questions.explanation: The head has no predecessor, so it is removed by moving head instead.

questions.stem:
What is the running time of this loop over a linked list of n nodes?

for i in range(len(ll)):
    total += ll[i]
questions.explanation: Each ll[i] walks i steps from the head: 0 + 1 + … + (n-1). Use for value in ll: for one O(n) walk.

questions.stem: Why is len(ll) O(1) in dsa/linked_list.py?
options: Python caches the length of every object
The list keeps _size up to date in every method that adds or removes
Linked lists have a fixed size
It is not — it walks the list
questions.explanation: A stored count, updated by push_front, append, insert_at, pop_front and remove. Forget one, and len lies.

questions.stem: Reversing a linked list in place needs how much extra space?
questions.explanation: Three references — prev, node and the saved next — whatever n is.

questions.stem: On 64-bit CPython, a Node with __slots__ takes about 48 bytes. One slot of an array of references takes:
options: it depends on the value stored
questions.explanation: One 8-byte reference per slot; the node is six times larger.

questions.stem: A doubly linked list can do in O(1) what a singly linked one cannot:
options: remove a node you already hold a reference to
questions.explanation: With prev in each node, the node itself gives you its predecessor. Indexing (a) and search (c) are still O(n).

questions.stem: What is a sentinel (dummy) node for?
options: to mark the end of the list instead of None
to give every real node a predecessor, removing the special case for the head
questions.explanation: With a permanent node before the first real one, removing the first real node looks exactly like removing any other.

questions.stem: A singly linked list with a tail reference. Removing the last node costs:
options: O(1) — the tail points at it
O(n) — the new last node must be found from the head
questions.explanation: After removing the last node, _tail must move to its predecessor, and only a walk from the head finds it in a singly linked list.

questions.stem: Python's collections.deque is implemented as:
options: a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks
a singly linked list of single values
questions.explanation: Blocks give array-like memory efficiency; the links give O(1) at both ends.

questions.stem: Why does the traversal loop test while node is not None: rather than while node.next is not None:?
options: The second version stops on the last node, so it never visits it — and crashes on an empty list
node.next is not allowed in a condition
questions.explanation: It is the standard off-by-one: node.next is not None is the right test only when you want to stop on the last node (to append after it).

questions.stem: After a = Node(1), b = Node(2, a), c = Node(3, b), what is c.next.next.value?
questions.explanation: c.next is b, and b.next is a, whose value is 1.

questions.stem: In Python, what happens to a node that nothing refers to any more?
options: it stays in memory until the program ends
questions.explanation: Unreachable objects are reclaimed automatically. del (b) only removes a name.

questions.stem: To insert a new node at index i ≥ 1, you walk to the node at index:
questions.explanation: The node at i − 1 is the one whose next must change. Index 0 is push_front.

questions.stem: Where in this course do short linked lists appear inside another structure?
options: as the chains of a hash table
questions.explanation: ChainingHashMap (Week 13) stores an Array of chains of Entry nodes.
